Most people hate networking because they think they have to sell themselves. You don't. My first piece of advice is to arrive early. When the room is still empty, it's much easier to talk to people. Second, don't talk about yourself for five minutes. Ask questions that invite the other person to talk, like: you were at the morning panel, weren't you? Then listen for common ground. Third, learn how to end a conversation. Many people stay too long because they don't know how to leave. Just say something positive, mention a next step, and say goodbye. It was great to meet you, let's keep in touch. That's all.

I'm an introvert. After two hours in a crowded room, I'm exhausted. So I created a simple method. At each reception, I plan only three good conversations. Not thirty. Three. My elevator pitch has two sentences: who I am, and one problem I solve for my clients. Then I ask questions, because people remember the person who listened to them, not the person who talked the most. And within twenty-four hours, I send a short message to each new contact, with one detail from our conversation. Most of my best clients came from those three conversations, or from a referral that started there.

Why do we remember some people and forget others? Researchers at a business school organized a networking event with two hundred participants. The next day, they asked everybody to write down the people they remembered, and why. The results were clear. People remembered a personal story or a shared interest, like a sport, a city or a problem at work. They also remembered people who asked them questions. Almost nobody remembered job titles. The lesson, say the researchers, is simple: if you want to be remembered, find common ground, and forget your title.
